title: Which graph tells the truth?
prompt: Both graphs show Garden A: 12 insects and Garden B: 15 insects. Which graph exaggerates the visual difference?
presenter: Give 20 seconds of silent thinking. Ask for one finger for Graph A or two for Graph B. Invite a 30-second neighbor explanation, then reveal the interpretation.
answer: Graph B exaggerates the difference. Its vertical axis begins at 10. Garden B has 3 more insects, or 25% more than Garden A—not 2.5 times as many. A zero baseline preserves bar-length comparisons of totals.
transition: The data stayed the same. The representation changed what we noticed. Next, make number relationships visible before asking students to calculate.

title: Make mathematics visible
prompt: Start at 4 on a number line and move 3 equal jumps to the right. Where do you land?
presenter: State the goal: explain addition as movement. Model the start at 4, predict, and reveal one jump at a time. Contrast counting the starting point as the first jump. Ask a neighbor to explain why there are 3 intervals, not 3 visited numbers.
answer: You land on 7: 4 → 5 → 6 → 7. The starting number is not a jump. Use objects or a drawing before the number line if needed.
transition: An accurate representation supports an accurate explanation. Now ask which representation fits a data question.

title: Investigate with GraphSplat
prompt: Which representation best shows how the same campus location changes temperature from 9 a.m. to noon to 3 p.m.?
presenter: Spend 7 minutes on the garden scale comparison, 6 minutes choosing a representation, and 7 minutes extending to a lesson. Launch GraphSplat and enter the garden CSV. Keep the local examples ready if Wi-Fi fails. Ask only one or two whole-room explanations.
answer: A line graph is useful for this question because the observations are ordered in time. Bars can compare readings, but a line emphasizes change. A pie chart suggests parts of a whole; a scatter plot is useful for relationships between paired numerical variables.
transition: Close the examples. What can we retrieve about choosing and interpreting graphs?

title: Check what sticks
prompt: Recall first. Explain your answer. Then check and revise.
presenter: Give about 45 seconds per question: silent recall, optional fingers or private note, neighbor explanation, reveal, revision. Use the remaining time to demonstrate how to build a similar recall set in Quiz and Flashcard Studio. Revisit with a different dataset in a later lesson.
answer: 1: A bar-chart baseline changes apparent bar-length ratios. 2: A line graph helps show change over time. 3: Explain 4 + 3 by three jumps from 4, ending at 7.
transition: A correct choice is a starting point. Plan how you will elicit and respond to explanations tomorrow.

title: ACE your math lesson
prompt: Articulate a strategy, connect it to a tool, and extend it to your own mathematical concept.
presenter: Give 2 minutes for an individual plan, 1 minute to share with a neighbor, and 2 minutes for a final revision and resource links. Invite a plan on paper or in the browser. No collection of responses.
answer: A useful plan names a mathematical goal, a strategy, a tool serving that goal, evidence of understanding, and a next task in a new context.
transition: Open the resource library and download the packet. The activities remain available after the convention.
